opus-5.5.text:
I think latent-space reasoning is very promising, though it's still early. The basic intuition is simple. When a model reasons in natural language, as in chain-of-thought, every step has to be squeezed into discrete tokens. Language is great for communicating with humans, but it isn't necessarily the most efficient medium for thinking. Many tokens in a reasoning trace exist mainly to keep the text fluent, and only a few carry the key decisions.

In our work on continuous thought, sometimes called Coconut, we let the model feed its hidden state back in as the next input, instead of committing to a specific word. Something interesting happens. A continuous thought can hold several possible next steps at once, almost like a superposition. So instead of committing early to one path, as greedy chain-of-thought does, the model can effectively do something closer to breadth-first search in latent space, keeping multiple candidates alive and pruning them gradually. On some planning and logical reasoning tasks, this gave better accuracy with far fewer tokens.

Theoretically, this matters too. You can show that for certain problems, such as graph reachability, continuous thoughts can be much more expressive per step than discrete tokens. So it isn't just an engineering trick. There's a real representational advantage.

There are serious open questions, though. First, training is hard. You don't have natural supervision for what the latent thoughts should be, so you often need curricula that start from language reasoning and gradually replace it with latent steps. Scaling that up to frontier-size models and general domains isn't solved. Second, interpretability and safety. One nice property of language chain-of-thought is that humans can read it, at least partially, and monitor it. If reasoning moves fully into latent space, we lose that window, and that's a real tradeoff the community has to think about. Third, it isn't yet clear how well this combines with reinforcement learning, which is currently the main driver of reasoning progress.

So my view is that the long-term answer is probably a hybrid. Models would think in latent space where it's efficient and verbalize at key points where we need checkability or communication. Humans work similarly: much of our thinking isn't in words, and we use language to organize and explain it. I'd say latent reasoning is one of the more fundamental directions, because it questions whether reasoning has to be tied to tokens at all.

r001.rationale: The response says continuous thoughts can be “much more expressive per step than discrete tokens,” conveying greater per-step capacity than language tokens in principle.

r002.rationale: It says a continuous thought can hold “several possible next steps at once,” like a superposition, keeping multiple candidates alive.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think latent-space reasoning is one of the most promising directions right now, but I want to be careful about why.

The current paradigm is chain-of-thought: the model reasons by writing tokens, one after another, in natural language. That works remarkably well, and it has a huge advantage, which is that we can read it. But it also has a cost. Every intermediate step has to be squeezed through a discrete bottleneck. You pick one token, you commit to it, and you move on. Human thinking isn't like that. When you're working on a hard problem, you often hold several possibilities in your head at once, and you only verbalize after things have settled. Language is the output of thinking, not the medium of it.

That's the intuition behind our work on Coconut, chain of continuous thought. Instead of decoding a token at each step, you feed the last hidden state back in as the next input. The model reasons in its own representation space. And what we saw is quite interesting: the continuous thought behaves a bit like a superposition. It can encode multiple candidate paths simultaneously, and the model effectively does a kind of breadth-first search without being explicitly told to. On tasks that need planning or backtracking, like certain graph-reachability problems, that turns out to be much more efficient than committing early in language.

So the promise is real: fewer tokens, more parallel exploration, and a reasoning process that isn't constrained by the vocabulary of English.

But I'd temper the enthusiasm in a few ways. First, training is hard. Pretraining data is all text, so there's no natural supervision for what a good latent thought looks like. We used curriculum learning to gradually replace language steps with continuous ones, and that works at small scale, but whether it scales cleanly to frontier models is still an open question. Second, you lose interpretability. If the reasoning is a vector, you can't just read it, and for safety and debugging that matters a lot. Third, there's a deeper question of whether the model actually learns to search in latent space or just learns to compress a shortcut. Those look similar on benchmarks and are very different in principle.

My honest view is that the future is probably hybrid. Latent reasoning for the fast, exploratory, parallel part, and language for the part where you commit, communicate, and let someone check your work. Language is a wonderful interface. It just shouldn't be the only place thinking is allowed to happen.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts committing to one discrete language token with a continuous thought that can encode multiple candidate paths, communicating greater information capacity per latent step.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says continuous thought behaves like a superposition and can encode multiple candidate paths simultaneously.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising direction. Today, when a language model reasons, it often produces a sequence of words, and each new step builds on those words. But that raises a question: does every intermediate step of reasoning need to be expressed in language? Maybe the model can do some of that computation in its internal representations and only translate the result into words when it needs to communicate.

That could give us more flexibility. Language is useful for expressing concepts, but it also forces you to commit to a particular formulation. In a latent space, the model might be able to maintain several possibilities or represent information that is difficult to express concisely in words. Potentially, that could make reasoning more efficient.

The challenge is how to train it. If a model generates intermediate text, we can inspect those steps and sometimes provide feedback on them. With latent reasoning, it’s harder to know whether an internal step represents useful progress. Simply running more computation in a hidden space doesn’t guarantee better reasoning. You need a training signal that encourages the model to use that computation productively.

So I’m optimistic, but I would distinguish the potential from what we can demonstrate. The important test is whether it solves harder problems more reliably for a given computational budget. A hybrid approach seems attractive: use internal computation where it helps, and language where explicit steps, verification, or interaction are useful.

r001.rationale: The candidate says latent space might represent information that is difficult to express concisely in words, but does not state that one latent token can carry more information than one language token.

r002.rationale: It mentions maintaining several possibilities in a latent space, but does not say that a single latent token simultaneously represents multiple alternative lines of reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think latent-space reasoning is a promising direction because language may not be the best representation for every intermediate step of a problem. When we solve something, we don’t necessarily put every thought into words. A model could also do some computation in a continuous internal representation and translate the result into language when it needs to communicate.

That gives you a potential advantage in efficiency, but it also creates a training challenge. With a text-based chain of thought, you have intermediate steps that you can inspect and sometimes supervise. In latent space, how do you know whether an additional computation step is making progress? How do you prevent the model from taking a shortcut that works on training examples but fails on harder problems?

So I would distinguish the potential from what we have demonstrated. A compact internal representation could be very useful, but being continuous or hidden doesn’t automatically make it good at reasoning. You still need to show that the model can plan, correct mistakes, and generalize—and that it does those things better for the same computational budget.

My guess is that a hybrid approach is quite natural: use latent computation for some internal processing, and use language when explicit steps, external tools, or human feedback are valuable. The important question is how to train those pieces to work together.

r001.rationale: The response says latent computation may be more efficient, but does not state that a latent token can carry more information than a language token.

r002.rationale: The response mentions internal latent computation but does not say a single latent token can represent multiple alternative lines of reasoning simultaneously.
